requirement:
A tracked read of an HC GitHub issue node records its identity and a fingerprint
of the supplied title, opening post, and status under
{cite}`requirements.sdk.graph.evidence.node_inputs`.
Changing any of those supplied fields changes the fingerprint under the same
fingerprinting rules. The fingerprint excludes cache fetch time and TTL;
refetching otherwise unchanged issue contents does not change it.

The fingerprint describes the issue contents supplied under HC's
[redaction policy](../authoring.md#habeas-req-requirements.authoring.redaction),
including the text presented to an agent.
rationale:
`references` for `requirements.sdk.habeas.github_nodes.inputs` returns no {impl}, {test} or {cite} sites. No test exercises the requirement's obligations:
- A tracked read records the issue's identity and a fingerprint.
- Changing the title, opening post or status changes the fingerprint.
- The fingerprint excludes fetch time and TTL.
- The fingerprint covers the contents supplied under HC's redaction policy.

That is a real test-adequacy gap.

The gap is acknowledged. `src/sdk.rs#enum[HabeasNode]` carries a {fixme} naming `requirements.sdk.habeas.github_nodes.inputs`. Its body says tests do not yet cover redacted contents, field-sensitive fingerprints, or fetch-time/TTL independence. It names nikomatsakis/habeas-codicem#26, which is open. The sibling {fixme} for `requirements.sdk.habeas.github_nodes` says identity and contents have no implementation or tests. Together these cover the missing tests, including the identity and fingerprint recording.

The cited `requirements.sdk.graph.evidence.node_inputs` is context only and was not reassessed. The acknowledged gap still exists, so the {fixme} is not stale.

Finishing a verification includes every successful tracked node read in its
`Fingerprinted`, whether ordinary code or a model tool requested it. Each observation
contains the node identity and the fingerprint of the contents actually supplied.
A failed read returns an error without inventing a successful observation.
Repeating an identical observation adds no information. Reading the same
identity with two different fingerprints preserves both observations.
